opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the starting point wasn't "let's start a company." The starting point was vLLM itself. When the project began at Berkeley, it was a research effort around PagedAttention, and then it grew much faster than any of us expected. At some point you look around and realize this open-source project is running inference for a huge number of companies and models, and the question becomes: how do we keep this thing healthy and moving fast for the long term?

Simon and I talked about this a lot. Academic funding and volunteer time can carry a project to a certain point. But once you have hardware vendors, model labs, cloud providers, and lots of end users all depending on it, the maintenance load is huge. Every week there are new models, new hardware, new kernels, new parallelism strategies. Someone has to coordinate all of that full-time, and do it well.

So for us, starting a company was about building a sustainable home for the people who work on vLLM, so the core contributors can focus on it without worrying about whether it fits into a PhD timeline or a side project.

The thing we were most careful about was the relationship between the company and the open-source project. We didn't want the company to "own" vLLM in a way that makes other contributors feel like second-class citizens. A big part of vLLM's value is that it's neutral. NVIDIA, AMD, Google, Intel, and many model companies all contribute, and they do that because they trust it isn't controlled by a competitor. So our principle was that the open-source project comes first, and the company has to create value in a way that strengthens the ecosystem rather than fencing it off.

On a personal level, Simon and I complement each other quite well. Simon has a strong sense of the product and the community, how people actually use vLLM in production, and I spend a lot of my time deep in the system internals: compilation, the execution path, performance. Starting something together felt natural because we'd already been working closely for a long time. The company is more like formalizing something we were already doing.

And to be honest, there's also the timing. Inference is becoming one of the most important layers in AI infrastructure. As models get deployed everywhere, the cost and efficiency of inference really matter. We felt that if we didn't seize this moment to invest seriously in vLLM, we'd regret it.

r001.rationale: The response says Simon and Kaichao complement each other, but does not say Kaichao would not start the company alone or that a solo founding team would be insufficient.

r002.rationale: It says the company would provide a sustainable home so contributors could focus on vLLM and help keep the project healthy and moving for the long term.

r003.rationale: The response explains why they founded the company, but does not distinguish agreement that vLLM needed a company from uncertainty about whether they themselves should found it.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it was never a "let's start a company" moment. It grew out of the project itself.

When I first got involved with vLLM, I was still a PhD student at Tsinghua, and I came to it as a contributor, mostly working on things like torch.compile integration and distributed inference. Simon, as you know, was leading the project at Berkeley with Woosuk. What I noticed over time was that the demand on the project was growing much faster than what a volunteer, academic-style team could sustain. Every week there was a new model, a new hardware backend, a new company putting vLLM into production and then hitting edge cases that nobody had time to look at.

So the real question we kept coming back to wasn't "should we make money from this," it was "how do we keep vLLM healthy." An open-source project at that scale needs people who can work on it full time, who can own the roadmap, who can say no to things, and who can make long-term bets like a proper compilation stack or better scheduling, instead of just fixing whatever broke yesterday. Grants and goodwill can carry you for a while, but not forever.

Simon and I talked about this a lot. We both felt strongly that vLLM had to stay open and stay neutral. The ecosystem trusts it because it's not tied to one vendor or one cloud. So any company we built had to be structured around that principle: the project comes first, the company exists to support it, not to capture it. That's actually what made it feel reasonable to me. If the plan had been to wrap it in something proprietary, I wouldn't have been interested.

The other thing that convinced me was the people. By that point we had worked together through a lot of difficult technical problems, late-night debugging across time zones, big refactors. You learn what someone is like under pressure. I trusted Simon, and I think that trust mattered more than any business plan.

So, in short, it was less an entrepreneurial decision and more a responsibility decision. The project needed a sustainable home, and we felt we were in a position to build one.

r001.rationale: The response discusses trust in Simon and the need for a sustainable home, but does not say Kaichao would not found the company alone or that the team would be insufficient.

r002.rationale: It says vLLM needed full-time support and a sustainable home to keep the project healthy and support its long-term development.

r003.rationale: The response describes agreement on supporting vLLM through a company, but does not express uncertainty about whether they themselves should found it.

astra-6.text:
For me, the main question was: how do we make vLLM successful over the long term? An open-source project needs more than good ideas. It needs people who can spend time maintaining it, improving reliability, and understanding what users actually need in production.

So, thinking about starting a company with Simon, I would frame it around that: can we build a sustainable business that also makes the open-source project stronger? There’s a lot of work between having a powerful inference engine and making it easy for people to operate. That’s where I see an opportunity, as long as we keep the community’s trust and make sure the company and the project reinforce each other.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the starting point was really vLLM itself—how do we make it more useful, and how do we help people run it in production? An open-source project can give you a great foundation, but there’s still a lot of work between having the software and operating a reliable service.

So the way I thought about starting a company with Simon was: can we build a team that focuses on that gap, while continuing to invest in the open-source project? Those two things need to reinforce each other. The company should create value around vLLM, and its success should also help us make vLLM better.
